title: Decomposers and Matter Cycling Core Test
description: Trace matter through dead material, decomposers, air, soil, and plants using evidence and system boundaries.

questions.prompt: A fallen leaf becomes smaller over months. Which account best conserves its matter?
questions.questionText: A fallen leaf becomes smaller over months. Which account best conserves its matter?
options: Its atoms are mostly converted into sunlight.
Its atoms stop existing once the leaf is invisible.
Its atoms move into organisms, gases, water, and soil substances.
All its atoms stay in the same recognizable leaf shape.
questions.correctAnswer: Its atoms move into organisms, gases, water, and soil substances.
questions.explanation: Matter changes form and location; disappearance from view is not destruction.

questions.prompt: Which observation best identifies a decomposer's role?
questions.questionText: Which observation best identifies a decomposer's role?
options: A plant captures light to build sugars.
A hawk catches a living mouse.
A fungus obtains nutrients by breaking down dead wood.
A rock breaks into smaller pieces after freezing.
questions.correctAnswer: A fungus obtains nutrients by breaking down dead wood.
questions.explanation: Decomposers obtain matter and energy from dead material or waste; weathering alone is not biological decomposition.

questions.prompt: In dead leaves -> fungus -> carbon dioxide, what does the last arrow represent?
questions.questionText: In dead leaves -> fungus -> carbon dioxide, what does the last arrow represent?
options: Carbon leaving the fungus during cellular respiration.
Light energy turning into carbon atoms.
The fungus performing photosynthesis.
All leaf minerals evaporating into air.
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon leaving the fungus during cellular respiration.
questions.explanation: Respiration releases some carbon from food molecules as carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Which pair correctly separates matter from energy during decomposition?
questions.questionText: Which pair correctly separates matter from energy during decomposition?
options: Carbon atoms can cycle; energy is transferred and some leaves as heat.
Carbon atoms become heat; energy becomes soil minerals.
Carbon and energy both return to plants as sunlight.
Carbon and energy both disappear when leaves decay.
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon atoms can cycle; energy is transferred and some leaves as heat.
questions.explanation: Matter is conserved while energy is transferred, with heat dispersing to the surroundings.

questions.prompt: A leaf breaks into tiny pieces when rubbed. What has this observation established?
questions.questionText: A leaf breaks into tiny pieces when rubbed. What has this observation established?
options: All carbon in the leaf has become carbon dioxide.
Decomposers must have caused the breakage.
Fragmentation occurred; biological decomposition has not been demonstrated.
The leaf's mineral nutrients are all ready for roots.
questions.correctAnswer: Fragmentation occurred; biological decomposition has not been demonstrated.
questions.explanation: Smaller pieces are evidence of physical breakage, not proof of microbial chemical changes.

questions.prompt: A plant obtains mineral nutrients released during decomposition. Where does most carbon for its new sugars come from?
questions.questionText: A plant obtains mineral nutrients released during decomposition. Where does most carbon for its new sugars come from?
options: Mineral particles absorbed through roots.
Heat from decomposing leaves.
Water molecules taken up by roots.
Carbon dioxide taken in during photosynthesis.
questions.correctAnswer: Carbon dioxide taken in during photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Minerals are important, but carbon in plant sugars comes primarily from carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Equal dry leaf samples begin at 20 g. After four weeks, moist-site samples average 12 g and dry-site samples 18 g, measured dry again. Which comparison is supported?
questions.questionText: Equal dry leaf samples begin at 20 g. After four weeks, moist-site samples average 12 g and dry-site samples 18 g, measured dry again. Which comparison is supported?
options: The moist-site samples lost 12 g more dry mass.
The moist-site samples lost 6 g more dry mass.
The dry-site samples lost 18 g of dry mass.
Both treatments lost the same dry mass.
questions.correctAnswer: The moist-site samples lost 6 g more dry mass.
questions.explanation: Losses are 8 g and 2 g; the difference is 6 g. Dry measurements reduce water-content confusion.

questions.prompt: A fresh leaf weighs 5 g and weighs 2 g after drying overnight. Why is this weak evidence for decomposition?
questions.questionText: A fresh leaf weighs 5 g and weighs 2 g after drying overnight. Why is this weak evidence for decomposition?
options: Much of the decrease could be water evaporating.
Drying must have destroyed the leaf's atoms.
A lighter leaf necessarily has more decomposers.
A mass measurement cannot detect any change.
questions.correctAnswer: Much of the decrease could be water evaporating.
questions.explanation: Water loss can reduce mass without biological breakdown, so the mechanism is not established.

questions.prompt: To test moisture effects on leaf decomposition, which comparison is strongest?
questions.questionText: To test moisture effects on leaf decomposition, which comparison is strongest?
options: Different leaf types and moisture; same container color.
Same leaf type, dry starting mass, temperature, and time; different moisture.
Same leaf type but different temperature, time, and moisture.
Same wet mass but different leaf types, moisture, and duration.
questions.correctAnswer: Same leaf type, dry starting mass, temperature, and time; different moisture.
questions.explanation: Keeping other relevant variables similar helps isolate moisture's effect.

questions.prompt: A model ends at dead plants -> decomposers. Which addition helps show matter cycling back into living plants?
questions.questionText: A model ends at dead plants -> decomposers. Which addition helps show matter cycling back into living plants?
options: Decomposers -> heat -> plant roots as food.
Decomposers -> sunlight -> green leaves.
Decomposers -> disappearance of all atoms.
Decomposers -> mineral nutrients in soil -> plant roots.
questions.correctAnswer: Decomposers -> mineral nutrients in soil -> plant roots.
questions.explanation: Mineral release and root uptake close one matter pathway; heat is not a material nutrient.

questions.prompt: Leaf litter builds up faster during a cold season. Which explanation is consistent with slower decomposition?
questions.questionText: Leaf litter builds up faster during a cold season. Which explanation is consistent with slower decomposition?
options: Cold changes leaf carbon into a different element.
Lower temperature can slow decomposer activity.
Fallen leaves stop containing chemical energy.
Cold prevents any physical movement of matter.
questions.correctAnswer: Lower temperature can slow decomposer activity.
questions.explanation: Temperature can affect biological reaction rates; it does not change carbon into another element.

questions.prompt: In a classroom dataset, a shaded soil sample releases carbon dioxide with no green plants present. What process could account for it?
questions.questionText: In a classroom dataset, a shaded soil sample releases carbon dioxide with no green plants present. What process could account for it?
options: Photosynthesis by the soil minerals.
Respiration by organisms using organic matter.
Conversion of shade directly into carbon.
Root uptake producing carbon from water.
questions.correctAnswer: Respiration by organisms using organic matter.
questions.explanation: Soil organisms can respire and release carbon dioxide even without green plants.

questions.prompt: Why should a food-web model include arrows from dead material at several feeding levels to decomposers?
questions.questionText: Why should a food-web model include arrows from dead material at several feeding levels to decomposers?
options: Decomposers receive matter only from top predators.
Decomposers create new energy for every feeding level.
Waste and remains from many organisms supply decomposers.
Every organism must be eaten alive before its matter can cycle.
questions.correctAnswer: Waste and remains from many organisms supply decomposers.
questions.explanation: Decomposition connects multiple parts of a food web, not just its top.

questions.prompt: A forest has less leaf litter after a windy week. Which measurement most helps distinguish transport from decomposition?
questions.questionText: A forest has less leaf litter after a windy week. Which measurement most helps distinguish transport from decomposition?
options: Measuring only the remaining litter's color.
Collecting and measuring leaves blown outside the study area.
Counting trees once after the wind.
Measuring the study area's sunlight once.
questions.correctAnswer: Collecting and measuring leaves blown outside the study area.
questions.explanation: Wind can move leaves across the system boundary; tracking that export tests an alternative explanation.

questions.prompt: A model ecosystem receives light but exchanges no matter with its surroundings. What can still leave it?
questions.questionText: A model ecosystem receives light but exchanges no matter with its surroundings. What can still leave it?
options: Carbon atoms carried by escaping gas.
Mineral nutrients through runoff.
Water vapor escaping through an opening.
Energy as heat.
questions.correctAnswer: Energy as heat.
questions.explanation: A boundary closed to matter need not be closed to energy. This is a model, not an instruction to seal living organisms.

questions.prompt: Decomposer activity drops while leaf fall stays the same. Which short-term change is most likely, assuming other conditions stay similar?
questions.questionText: Decomposer activity drops while leaf fall stays the same. Which short-term change is most likely, assuming other conditions stay similar?
options: More dead material accumulates and nutrient release slows.
Less dead material accumulates because fewer organisms use it.
All plants immediately stop photosynthesis.
Mineral supply necessarily increases at the same rate as before.
questions.correctAnswer: More dead material accumulates and nutrient release slows.
questions.explanation: With the input unchanged and breakdown slower, litter tends to accumulate; plant responses need not be immediate.

questions.prompt: Two sites lose equal leaf mass, but one loses leaves to runoff. Which conclusion is justified?
questions.questionText: Two sites lose equal leaf mass, but one loses leaves to runoff. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Equal mass loss does not prove equal decomposition rates.
The sites must have identical decomposer activity.
Runoff is a form of cellular respiration.
All loss at both sites must be biological.
questions.correctAnswer: Equal mass loss does not prove equal decomposition rates.
questions.explanation: Mass loss can have several pathways; transport must be separated from breakdown.

questions.prompt: Three moist samples lose 7, 8, and 9 g; three dry samples lose 1, 2, and 3 g under otherwise matched conditions. What strengthens the moisture claim?
questions.questionText: Three moist samples lose 7, 8, and 9 g; three dry samples lose 1, 2, and 3 g under otherwise matched conditions. What strengthens the moisture claim?
options: Only the largest moist loss matters.
The number 9 proves all moist habitats behave identically.
The averages remove the need to consider any other variable.
The treatment difference repeats across independent samples.
questions.correctAnswer: The treatment difference repeats across independent samples.
questions.explanation: Consistent differences across replicates support the result, while generalization still has limits.

questions.prompt: A labeled carbon atom starts in a dead leaf and later appears in a new plant's sugar. Which route is plausible?
questions.questionText: A labeled carbon atom starts in a dead leaf and later appears in a new plant's sugar. Which route is plausible?
options: Leaf -> heat -> plant root -> sugar.
Leaf -> decomposer -> carbon dioxide -> photosynthesis -> sugar.
Leaf -> mineral nitrogen -> photosynthesis -> sugar.
Leaf -> water molecule -> sugar without any carbon input.
questions.correctAnswer: Leaf -> decomposer -> carbon dioxide -> photosynthesis -> sugar.
questions.explanation: The carbon atom can return through respiration and photosynthesis without becoming energy or a different element.

questions.prompt: A student measures only the leaf pile and says its mass loss violates conservation. What is missing?
questions.questionText: A student measures only the leaf pile and says its mass loss violates conservation. What is missing?
options: An assumption that every leaf atom remains in the pile.
A rule that conservation applies only to rocks.
Matter transferred to gases, organisms, water, or outside the pile.
A way to convert missing grams directly into heat.
questions.correctAnswer: Matter transferred to gases, organisms, water, or outside the pile.
questions.explanation: Conservation applies to the whole tracked system; measuring one compartment misses transfers.

questions.prompt: An airtight theoretical system has 100 units of tracked carbon: 60 in leaves, 20 in organisms, 20 in gas. Later leaves contain 35 and organisms 25. How many units must be in gas if these are the only pools?
questions.questionText: An airtight theoretical system has 100 units of tracked carbon: 60 in leaves, 20 in organisms, 20 in gas. Later leaves contain 35 and organisms 25. How many units must be in gas if these are the only pools?
options: 40 units.
65 units.
20 units.
35 units.
questions.correctAnswer: 40 units.
questions.explanation: Total tracked carbon stays 100; 100 - 35 - 25 = 40.

questions.prompt: A model returns both mineral nutrients and heat from decomposers to plant roots as building materials. Which correction is needed?
questions.questionText: A model returns both mineral nutrients and heat from decomposers to plant roots as building materials. Which correction is needed?
options: Keep both arrows because heat contains mineral atoms.
Remove both arrows because decomposers release nothing.
Keep the mineral arrow; show heat dispersing as energy rather than root building material.
Keep only the heat arrow because roots absorb energy instead of minerals.
questions.correctAnswer: Keep the mineral arrow; show heat dispersing as energy rather than root building material.
questions.explanation: Minerals supply matter. Heat is energy, not a substance that roots build into tissue.

questions.prompt: Warm, moist leaves lose mass faster than cold, dry leaves. Can this test establish the effect of temperature alone?
questions.questionText: Warm, moist leaves lose mass faster than cold, dry leaves. Can this test establish the effect of temperature alone?
options: Yes; the warmer group always isolates temperature.
No; moisture also changed and could affect the result.
No; decomposition cannot be measured by any experiment.
Yes; temperature and moisture are the same variable.
questions.correctAnswer: No; moisture also changed and could affect the result.
questions.explanation: Two changed factors make their individual contributions unclear.

questions.prompt: A stream gains much dead organic material. Oxygen falls as microbial respiration increases. Which chain best explains this?
questions.questionText: A stream gains much dead organic material. Oxygen falls as microbial respiration increases. Which chain best explains this?
options: More organic food -> more photosynthesis in all microbes -> oxygen loss.
More dead material -> oxygen atoms destroyed -> lower oxygen.
More decomposition -> less microbial activity -> lower oxygen.
More organic food -> more aerobic respiration -> more oxygen use.
questions.correctAnswer: More organic food -> more aerobic respiration -> more oxygen use.
questions.explanation: Aerobic decomposers use oxygen; this can link a material input to oxygen availability for other organisms.

questions.prompt: A mesh bag loses 10 g of leaf dry mass. Fragments collected beneath it total 6 g. What can be said about the 10 g loss?
questions.questionText: A mesh bag loses 10 g of leaf dry mass. Fragments collected beneath it total 6 g. What can be said about the 10 g loss?
options: Exactly 10 g was chemically decomposed.
Exactly 6 g became carbon dioxide.
At least 6 g left as fragments; the full 10 g cannot be assigned to decomposition.
No matter crossed the bag boundary.
questions.correctAnswer: At least 6 g left as fragments; the full 10 g cannot be assigned to decomposition.
questions.explanation: Collected fragments demonstrate physical export; remaining loss needs further evidence.

questions.prompt: Two models both show leaves disappearing. Model A sends all matter to soil; Model B includes soil, organisms, and gases. Why prefer B?
questions.questionText: Two models both show leaves disappearing. Model A sends all matter to soil; Model B includes soil, organisms, and gases. Why prefer B?
options: It proves every atom follows the same route.
It shows that decomposition creates carbon atoms.
It requires no measurements because it has more arrows.
It accounts for several plausible destinations of leaf atoms.
questions.correctAnswer: It accounts for several plausible destinations of leaf atoms.
questions.explanation: A more complete accounting includes gaseous products and decomposer biomass, while still requiring testing.

questions.prompt: Carbon dioxide rises in both a leaf-and-soil treatment and a soil-only comparison. What would strengthen a claim that added leaves increase respiration?
questions.questionText: Carbon dioxide rises in both a leaf-and-soil treatment and a soil-only comparison. What would strengthen a claim that added leaves increase respiration?
options: Any rise in either container.
Using only the leaf treatment's final value.
Comparing different container volumes without adjustment.
A consistently greater rise in replicated leaf-and-soil treatments.
questions.correctAnswer: A consistently greater rise in replicated leaf-and-soil treatments.
questions.explanation: Soil alone can respire; the additional effect needs a matched comparison.

questions.prompt: A decomposer becomes food for another organism. Which explanation joins decomposition to energy pyramids?
questions.questionText: A decomposer becomes food for another organism. Which explanation joins decomposition to energy pyramids?
options: Chemical energy in decomposer biomass can transfer, with some energy dispersed as heat at each step.
Decomposers restart all lost heat as sunlight.
All energy in the dead leaf reaches the next consumer.
Energy transfer stops once matter enters decomposers.
questions.correctAnswer: Chemical energy in decomposer biomass can transfer, with some energy dispersed as heat at each step.
questions.explanation: Decomposers are part of energy flow, but they do not recycle dispersed heat back into sunlight.

questions.prompt: A fallen log remains recognizable for years. Does that disprove decomposition?
questions.questionText: A fallen log remains recognizable for years. Does that disprove decomposition?
options: No; decomposition rates vary and can be slow while material still remains.
Yes; decomposition must remove all material in a week.
Yes; recognizable objects cannot exchange matter.
No; all logs decay at exactly the same rate.
questions.correctAnswer: No; decomposition rates vary and can be slow while material still remains.
questions.explanation: Durable material and local conditions affect rates; persistence does not mean zero breakdown.

questions.prompt: A study finds less litter after adding a treatment, but it did not track runoff, fragments, or gases. Which conclusion best fits the evidence?
questions.questionText: A study finds less litter after adding a treatment, but it did not track runoff, fragments, or gases. Which conclusion best fits the evidence?
options: The treatment proved that atoms were destroyed.
The treatment reduced measured litter; the pathways of loss remain uncertain.
Every missing gram became soil minerals.
The treatment certainly increased biological decomposition by the full loss.
questions.correctAnswer: The treatment reduced measured litter; the pathways of loss remain uncertain.
questions.explanation: The measured outcome is clear, but the mechanism requires additional evidence.
